About what it means to call you son.

Blessings Tobi,
Today and in the years to come
May your kind heart
Continue to care deeply
Not afraid to love
Daring to give yourself
Your faithfulness to friends
It will be your legacy.

Blessings Tobi,
For your kind eyes
You see what others miss,
For your love of family
Your steadfast commitment
Your gentle spirit
That speaks louder than words.

To my beloved Son,
My father’s heart breaks open
Again, today,
You fill my heart with joy.
Be blessed.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: Tobi’s Blessing - After 21 years

items.text:
Blessings Whitney for thirty years of life,
From the moment you were born, I knew you.
The fun loving young girl with a skinned nose (From our first holiday together)
The teenage adventures,
With friends and the beach
History connecting families
Through sharing life
For a child that has emerged
To become a beautiful young woman.

Your beauty begins with your laugh,
My life is richer with our shared stories
And the bits you know about the Gribbles
That no one else could ever know
Blessing for your love, for my children
For your heart that has found joy in them.

I pray for your eyes to be open to possibilities.
As seasons come and go in your life
May you embrace the momentary sadnesses
And seek the truth in what they say
Finding the joy in how love transforms everything.

May you be a blessing to others
As you bring joy to their lives
I pray for an open heart
That is willing to take time to reflect
I pray for your deepest loves
They will direct you to explore life in all its fullness.

May grace and peace surround your life
Beloved Whitney
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: Whitney’s Blessing

items.text:
The accuser screams,
You are worthless,
Harsh words echo
Deeply wounding
Seeking despair
Attacking weakness
Betraying confidence
Desiring revenge

A voice of pain
Anxious uncertainty
Self destructive
Wishing hate
Empty hope
Suffering
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: My Accuser’s Voice

items.text:
Alone is feeling a tear roll down my cheek,
Knowing this is my sadness,
That only I can feel,
Only I have loved this way,
What I feel, alone,
Love and sadness slowly winding down,
Seeking a path through,
Till, finally, the tear leaves my cheek,
And falls,
Joining my sadnesses,
I am alone.

Alone is the lonely path in the wilderness,
Knowing this is my path,
That only I can tread,
Only I can take the next step forward,
What I feel, alone,
My thoughts and uncertainties,
Seeking the light,
Till I am blinded,
And I stumble forward
Another step,
I am alone.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: Alone

items.text:
What future was imagined?
Splintered into a million drops of vapour,
Leaving nothing that can be grasped,
I question what was reality,
The drops of moisture remind me,
With the beads that collected,
Of dreams broken and tears shed,
And, what can never be remembered,
In the same way again.

Broken dreams are etched in my heart,
Forgetting is my heart’s desire,
Memories that keep me awake,
Regret is an easy refuge,
To evade the blows that were the breaking,
Remembering is the anxious,
Pursuit of Why?
Never to dream is the only way,
To never be broken again.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: Where do broken dreams take me?

items.text:
For every courageous act
First flutters the wings of doubt
Beating against my weak will,
My lack of faith a closed heart
Trust - Perhaps now
Is your moment to be free.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: Trust

items.text:
Gazing through the leafy sky
A space found to lie down and look up
Still and waiting
Yesterday slowly peeling away,
Tomorrow being pushed back to now,
Now, a gentler space,
Awake but not fully,
Conscious but dozing
Peace slowly landing
Today is doing her work
Tomorrow will come soon enough
Now, I listen to what today says to me
As I look beyond the trees into the sky
I wonder did I see it part just a little
Was it an echo I heard?
Here is my child, now, My beloved.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: Dozing

items.text:
Faith love and hope
Three horsemen riding
through my life
Triumphant, triumvirate
Defeated unless there is;
Someone to trust in
Someone I love deeply
Someone to hope with;
Faith, love and hope
Don’t belong to me
They are between us
Shared in a poem
Or in a longing gaze
Or that special word
Or a soft touch;
Faith hope and love
Belong in understanding
Shared wistfully, knowing
they can never be satisfied
Holding disappointment
Cherishing this moment
that we hold together.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: Faith, love and hope

items.text:
A tear left to wind
A lonely track
down my cheek
Exposing a vulnerable moment
Is allowed to stay
As an act of trust
That asks a question
Is this where I belong?
Will you notice? Or,
will this tear be lost,
My pain forgotten
In the rush of everyone
Going to where they belong.

A smile offered
To a painful secret
Opening trust
Hurt locked away
Because, it says I don’t belong
Given in a shared moment
A gentle smile
Is an outstretched hand
That draws the secret closer
Reassuring when my
dark fears are exposed
That intimate secret
Brought to light
Together here we belong.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: Be where I belong

items.text: As uncomfortable as I sometimes feel about my faith in God and how some Christians express their faith, I still find it the most believable way to direct my life, providing meaning and purpose to how I know myself. I am very aware of how Christianity has failed historically again and again to live up to its ideals. This shouldn’t be too surprising. Even the apostle Paul wrote about the internal conflict he faced in doing the things that he didn’t want to do while at the same time not being able to do the good things he desired for God.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: The most believable way

items.text: I think about my small town country beginnings, growing up in a rural community where my relationship to the bigger cities feels like Kathmandu and its relationship to Delhi. There are things you don’t know what you don’t know when first venturing into a bigger world. My experience in Delhi mostly reflects my ignorance and the realisation of my need to be a learner.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: The need to be a learner

items.text: I reflect after that this may be one of the dumbest things I have ever done to combat human trafficking. I continue to feel conflicted about the whole experience. … There is no judgment, only prayer. The ethical dilemma is about the action that should occur to demonstrate love for our neighbour in this situation practically. I did what I was asked, which may be enough for this time.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: Only prayer

items.text: Sometimes, it’s very difficult to stand for what is right, especially when strong voices question the validity of the heart of what you do. … Despite being a minority in Australia, I believe in God and express that belief through my Christian faith. When I see the impact of injustice on someone powerless to fight back, it's important to stand up and do something about it.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: Standing for what is right

items.text: A seven day road trip on the roughest roads is a great place to start new relationships. We ate, talked, peed in the Nepali toilet and spent many hours in silence together. … And so, the foundations of relationships were formed in the space of a few days travelling over the dirt tracks and scattered potholed bitumen they call roads in Nepal. I, a foreigner, was quickly accepted into their world. This belonging felt like a community I wanted to be part of.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.source: My First Twelve Days in Nepal (autoethnography), 2023
items.title: The roughest roads

items.text: I realise this is because this is something that I have given my heart to, and I allowed myself to be vulnerable to the group when giving my presentation. My heart has a very tender, soft place for this role and its place in my life. I am prepared to admit that what this role asks me to do is closely tied to my identity.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.source: My First Twelve Days in Nepal (autoethnography), 2023
items.title: A tender, soft place

items.text: In recent years, I have been drifting from my evangelical notions of justice. This shift happened because of my experience of injustice, complete brokenness, and the process of restoration. Compassion is now the primary shaper of how I seek to respond to my world and is central to my formation of theology. Loving my neighbour has taken on new challenges as I have sought to respond with compassion, which has benefited from a growth in humility.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.source: My First Twelve Days in Nepal (autoethnography), 2023
items.title: Compassion as shaper

items.text: Despite my questions and uncertainties about my former theological props, I trust my calling to act justly and to bring healing to the world and its broken relationships. To seek out the virtuous path that leads me to discover more kindness and less judgement, more grace and less sin, more faith and less doubt.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.source: My First Twelve Days in Nepal (autoethnography), 2023
items.title: More kindness, less judgement

items.text: When I experience belonging, I need to test it for a while before I can trust it. I still bear the scars of isolation and aloneness from my childhood and teenage years. Even today, I still am surprised that people want to connect with me. My initial internal response is still seeing myself through that time when very few people wanted to associate with me.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.source: My First Twelve Days in Nepal (autoethnography), 2023
items.title: Testing belonging

items.text: He concluded by saying, “it’s no good saying that my pile of ashes is bigger than yours”. I made a call at that point to follow into ministry no matter what the cost. I wanted my life to be defined by my obedience. Not by the things that I have done. But, by how faithfully I have loved and forgiven and demonstrated compassion even in the midst of injustice.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: A bigger pile of ashes

items.text: Then, there is the ego that sits in this work. I have to admit I feel good about what I do. I get fulfilment from seeing the results and from helping people. I also know that too much ego can make this all about me, and I am aware of the dangers of pride and how it can quickly lead to my downfall. I have found that life brings about enough success to keep me going and enough failure to temper my natural optimism with a healthy dose of reality. Without this balance, I could quickly get caught up in my success rather than keep my focus on the source of success.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: Enough success, enough failure

items.text: This is a different phase of “calling.” It’s not the calling into a new land anymore with the tinge of excitement that comes from launching into something new. … But recently, I have considered that doing anything worthwhile will take a five-year commitment. When I listen to my inner voice telling me this, I know that this will be the reality of living a called life for me at this time.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: A different phase of calling

items.text: My vocation is best described as how I choose to love my neighbour. … I often comment on how much I love my work, realising that my work satisfaction is partly formed because of the misfortune of others. This seems grossly unfair to those who are exploited.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: How I choose to love

items.text: Rescue is an integral part of the Christian story. I believe that I have been rescued myself. It was a real experience of coming out of darkness and into light, restoring my relationship with God. This was not done without great cost.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: Out of darkness

items.text: My theology is understood in the ways I open myself up to the concept of God - My belief that this world isn’t a closed frame and that there is involvement by God. … Theology is formed in the space between what I believe and what I do. In my Christian life, I am reborn into practical theology. The core idea of being made in God’s image ensures that theology becomes a lived practice.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: Between belief and action

items.text: This dichotomy conflicts with my inner sense of right and wrong. But, even more so, it brings to the forefront one of the ongoing questions around the stated truths of the Christian God. He is all loving and all powerful, yet there remain questions about the existence of evil. The more I try to understand these two ideas and how they co-exist, the less certain I am about some of what I once considered foundational in my belief in God.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: Less certain

items.text: To help me make sense of life and my continued belief in God is to keep my theology simple. I have settled on a very simple character virtue I have sought to develop: being kind to others (how does that separate me from the rest of the world?). If others are not being kind, I need to advocate for the right thing to be done.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: A simple theology of kindness

items.text: Inherent in this lies the contradictions we find between orthodoxy and orthopraxy. (Right belief and right action). This sort of experience pushed my faith to the edges, beyond the safe confines of a Sunday Church service that was, for many years, the central activity of my Christian faith. It pushes me into a deeper understanding of some of Christ’s words. The challenge of loving God with all your heart actually means caring for your neighbour.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: Faith pushed to the edges

items.text: It seems strange that after such a restless life of always thinking about what’s next, these days, I wake up to a sense of contentedness. I don’t claim everything is perfect, but I am blessed with a sense of connection to my family, friends, faith, and work. Each of them brings a gift that I can celebrate every day.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: Waking to contentedness

items.text: The 50s started painfully. With the loss of my Dad, my life broke down with a mixture of burnout and depression and painfully reconstructing a healthier version of myself. Hopefully, it is a person much kinder and more compassionate than the one that preceded it.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: A kinder version of myself

items.text: I know that so often I am less than loving. I know that the person I love the most in this life, my wife April is also the one that bears the brunt of my unlovingness. God invites us into all his love, it’s a fierce, loyal, forgiving love. And, as I come into his presence, often I know there are things that will make him weep.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: A fierce, loyal, forgiving love

items.text: Yet as we cry together, about the shared loves that we have, I know that it's by being open to knowing the pain of disappointment that love can live more deeply in me. I am given that choice, to shy away and become less known to myself and to God. Or, to become more fully what God has intended me to become, the purpose that he created me for. To become love, to enter into God’s love and to stay in that presence.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: To become love

items.text: For me it meant being reduced sometimes to an almost childlike state of total dependence on others to be able to complete some of the simplest tasks such as buying a mobile phone, ensure that we have drinking water delivered or working out why we had no gas or why the power had gone off. … This was a humbling experience that reminded me of the need to not get too proud. I must never forget my dependence on God. That whatever I have today may not be here tomorrow. To tread lightly in this world because it’s a fleeting existence.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: Tread lightly

items.text: This was my first experience of working in a place with no spirit. In the end it was quite a soulless existence. My weight hovered at around 8 stone. I was constantly tired due to lack of sleep. I saw no hope and no future. My spirit was stripped away during these four years of abuse.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: A place with no spirit

items.text: The hardest journey that I have ever faced is the inward journey. It's the one that takes me to those places that I would rather not go to. God takes us there. If we truly desire greatness in the Kingdom then we must go to the place that we fear the most. If we are willing God will allow us to stare it in the face.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: The inward journey

items.text: Instead we took the kids to a park. We had a packed lunch prepared for the day at the Convention centre so it became a picnic day. After lunch we played in the playground and went for a walk. We wasted time together but it was lots of fun. … We are not poor, but we don’t have lots of spare cash. Like most families we need to watch how we spend our money. We try to live simply so we can spend time with our kids.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: Wasted time together

items.text: This I think is the most important lesson I have learned. That going to the footy every week is one of my most valuable inputs I have into my son’s life. When he asks me, “did I run forward this week, Dad”? My affirmation is vital for Toby. He needs to know that he has done exactly what I asked and I love watching his face light up when he is told he did well.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: Did I run forward?

items.text: I would describe my relationship with God as mixed. I continue to have no doubts about my faith. But, I continue to have lots of doubts about the church. I have little desire to engage in corporate worship, yet my heart lifts when I experience true community.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: My heart lifts

items.text: Driving past people living with no safety nets always invites me to consider how I spend the enormous privilege I’ve been given. My prayer continues to ask God this question. And at 58 years old, I want to ensure that my time is used wisely. I want my life to be seen as one of continued obedience to God’s call. … I know that as I sit on the brink of something new that God is inviting me into, I have never felt more ALIVE.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: On the brink of something new

items.text: A few weeks ago, I visited the church of my childhood. This was not a happy place for my spiritual growth. I witnessed the same people doing the same things they always had done in the church’s name. There was no challenge to their thinking, and the sermon was the same tired old story of us against them. I don’t want to live life like that.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: The church of my childhood

items.text: I remember after my Dad passed away early in the morning and as I sat in a park by myself, the bright sunlight, bird calls, and the noises of young families enjoying their discovery of the park were experienced through a fog. Something significant had ended in my world, but for everyone else, their world was rushing on. And, then, the tears came. I remember waking up for the first time, weeping uncontrollably. Each tear was an expression of the love I experienced with my Dad.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: Each tear

items.text: But, the reality of my faith continues in the midst of this as I pause to remember the sorrow experienced by those witnesses of Christ’s death. And, as I join them, I remember this is the price paid for me to experience the full impact of love. Without this moment, when God laid down his life for his beloved world, I would not be able to cry like I cried when Dad passed away, celebrate a love of 30+ years with my wife, or join others in a sacred community who are choosing to be witnesses to Good Friday today.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: Good Friday in Nepal

items.text: I realise that this doesn’t mean I won’t have experiences of belonging now. Instead, it strengthens my desire to change how I belong to others. I want my connection with people to feel kind, attentive and fully there with them in their moment. And the miracle is that my loneliness dissipates when I have a conversation marked with these qualities. When I see someone touched by my kindness, I realise I have connected and allowed that person to belong fully.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: Fully there in their moment

items.text: This family had so little but gave me an open heart. As important as my work is, life is always about everyday interactions. But these can contain the heart of God when they contain kindness and love. I was the recipient of love regularly. Even in beautiful Pokhara, I witnessed poverty and injustice. I am thankful for how close I came to it and the reminder of one of the marks of healing: to seek to be loving wherever I am. I write these words with gratitude for the privilege to serve, love, and seek justice.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: The heart of God in everyday things

items.text: Dealing with people brings a range of ethical questions. I could choose to deal with them through a simplistic moral/theological lens of a God who has strict guidelines about right and wrong. But, I can’t find this God. After 30 years of living as a Christian I am less certain today of where God’s boundaries sit in regards to behaviours. What I am finding is that as I get older my values are becoming more settled. When I am tempted to judge I want to look for the goodness in the other person. I want to see evil more clearly and respond to it more decisively. Even if that decision is to be more loving.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: I can’t find this God

items.text: But, I also realise that if I hadn’t had those disappointments I wouldn’t be where I am today. This helps me hear more clearly the words of Paul, in giving thanks for all things. In the midst of disappointment it’s hard to understand what God is doing. But, taking time to reflect allows me to better understand what happened in the past and provide perspective for my future. … I am thankful to be able to feel disappointment, because without that I never would know the full extent of my love.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: Thankful for disappointment

items.text: Arriving home felt strange. Our familiar house bears the scars of four kids growing up, numerous friends visiting, countless shared meals, robust loud conversations discussing every aspect of human existence, the odd fiery argument (usually with me) and lots of laughter. But, now our kids have left or are transitioning to a more independent life, and when returning home, the house feels much quieter.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: The quieter house

items.text: I realise that home is a place where I can be completely myself. I don’t have to put on any pretexts and am free to arrange things my way. … But home is that place where I can take off my shoes and, even if my feet smell, know this is ok. It’s that place where I can organise my routine my way. Home is a place of rest where all pretences are irrelevant. This also describes my hope for eternity. I am acutely aware of my flaws and how they restrict me, so I long for a place where I can be completely free. Where who I am is matched with what I desire to be.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: Where all pretences are irrelevant

items.text: For most people it isn’t a single act of abuse that destroys their soul. More often it’s the daily accumulation of barbs and jabs that slowly suck the life out of any productive activity. They are the thousand pinpricks that slowly accumulate and take away any passion that may be felt for the daily tasks needed to be done. Redemption is found when the gifts that are brought are celebrated by another.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: A thousand pinpricks

items.text: In this poem I was also exploring the beauty of creation and the discovery of my place in the Creator’s heart. The thought that the creator of this world would stop to listen to me, that he would hear my voice and know me by name inspires me to explore more of this Creator. Imagination is the place where a deeper experience of God begins.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: Known by name

items.text: It was one of those periods that I best describe as dark, or as if a fog had come over my life that limited any hope of finding a way forward. I couldn’t see any way to get myself out of it and its clammy tentacles infiltrated every part of my life. Although in many ways it was unpleasant I also recognise this was the beginning of a new conversation that allowed me to slowly emerge from this debilitating fog into a more hopeful life.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: Out of the fog

items.text: Uncertainty is the path to vulnerability. It’s the realisation as one writer expresses it, “that there is a God and you’re not it”. The truest outcome of being able to embrace uncertainty in ourselves is to become more compassionate towards our vulnerability so we are better equipped to fully enter into community. The uncomfortableness of uncertainty is not our enemy rather it’s the voice that speaks most clearly to our need to begin a conversation with God.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: Uncertainty is not our enemy

items.text: When I was depressed the one thing that I desired above all else was to sleep through the night. I dreaded going to sleep because I realised that I would wake too soon. I knew that I would wake with the problems of the day ahead tossing around my head. I felt like there was never any rest. … To be able to say tonight because God is watching over me that it doesn’t matter what else is going on I will sleep is a statement about the blessing that comes with being right with God. I am no longer alone but held safe where I belong.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: In peace I will sleep

items.text: Death is life’s ultimate equaliser. Whatever distinctions we construct between ourselves—wealth, status, achievement, influence—none of us escapes its finality. Perhaps this is why we are so interested in the final stages of another person’s life. We record last words, last meals, last wishes and final gestures, as though proximity to death gives ordinary things greater significance.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: The ultimate equaliser

items.text: This may be where hope is found, not in the promise that death will be painless or that its loneliness can be removed, but in the conviction that no manner of dying can take us where God has not already been. The person who dies must cross that final threshold alone, but they are not abandoned by God.
items.author: Chris Gribble
items.title: Where God has already been
